impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The decision has major implications for the scope of patent protection available for biologic drug claims, particularly antibody patents with genus claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce broad antibody patent claims, providing greater protection for innovative biologic drugs and their market exclusivity periods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug manufacturers face heightened barriers to invalidating antibody patents, potentially delaying market entry and increasing pharmaceutical costs.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license for commercialization—retains sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The decision clarifies standing requirements in complex patent licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing deals can retain litigation rights while monetizing patents through exclusive licenses, providing flexibility in patent portfolio management and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a broader universe of potential plaintiffs, as patent owners who have substantially licensed away their patent rights may still maintain standing to sue.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that four asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether the inventorship determination on related patents was properly supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that plaintiffs failed to establish that each asserted trade secret was protectable under California law because the information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity for incorrect inventorship and on breach of contract, but affirmed the counterfeiting claim and damages. This decision significantly raises the evidentiary bar for trade secret claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a reinforced requirement that plaintiffs must clearly establish protectable trade secrets with specificity, rather than relying on broadly defined confidential information.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face a higher burden to demonstrate that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry, potentially weakening enforcement of trade secret portfolios.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim was barred by the three-year statute of limitations, specifically when the limitations period began to run given Insulet's knowledge of the alleged misappropriation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This decision provides critical guidance on when the DTSA limitations clock starts running based on a plaintiff's constructive knowledge.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from a strict application of the DTSA statute of limitations, providing a clear defense when the trade secret owner had early knowledge of potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to suspect misappropriation, or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely due to the statute of limitations.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's damages expert testimony and damages models for trade secret misappropriation, and whether it erred in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the full jury verdict. The decision addresses permissible damages methodologies in trade secret cases involving complex software licensing relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and trade secret owners benefit from expanded flexibility in presenting damages models, including unjust enrichment theories, when seeking compensation for misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives to licensed software face continued exposure to substantial trade secret and breach of contract damages claims from former licensors.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court's use of a single verdict form question covering infringement across all asserted patents, and its jury instructions on § 101 patent eligibility, constituted reversible error.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was prejudicially deficient. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility for one patent while affirming eligibility for others. This decision reinforces the requirement for patent-specific jury findings in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that juries must make patent-specific infringement findings, preventing plaintiffs from obtaining damages across entire patent portfolios based on ambiguous verdicts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased trial complexity and the risk that verdict form deficiencies will result in vacated judgments and costly retrials.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not included in its prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in analyzing the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous proof that a skilled searcher would have discovered the prior art at issue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain greater ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions, as courts must carefully scrutinize estoppel arguments without hindsight bias.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a weakened estoppel shield, meaning that IPR proceedings may not fully foreclose defendants' invalidity challenges in subsequent litigation.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of doctrine of equivalents theories for a patent directed to multicore processor task allocation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the grant of summary judgment to Intel on extraterritoriality grounds while affirming on the doctrine of equivalents theory, and also reversed the striking of certain damages expert theories. The decision clarifies the territorial reach of U.S. patent law for semiconductor design activities and the standards for excluding damages testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a broader interpretation of the territorial scope of U.S. patent infringement for technology designed domestically but manufactured abroad, and from more permissive standards for damages expert testimony.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global design and manufacturing operations face expanded infringement exposure in U.S. courts for activities they may have considered extraterritorial.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony based on non-personal knowledge is admissible at summary judgment for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate witness may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code describing commands is not hearsay. This ruling has significant implications for how companies defend patent cases using historical corporate records and testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from expanded evidentiary tools, including 30(b)(6) testimony from witnesses without personal knowledge and direct use of source code as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to invalidity challenges based on historical corporate testimony and source code evidence, even when original witnesses are unavailable.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a patent specification constituted correction of an obvious typographical error entitled to priority from the earlier provisional application, or whether it introduced new matter that broke the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the patent specification was not an obvious typographical error and constituted new matter not supported by the provisional application. Because the priority chain was broken, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid®) anticipated the patent claims. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent prosecution and provisional application drafting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority requirements, ensuring that patentees cannot retroactively expand claim scope through corrections to provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies face severe consequences from drafting errors in provisional applications, as even seemingly minor typographical errors can break the priority chain and expose patents to anticipation by intervening disclosures.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for automated capture, processing, and sharing of farming data are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285 should be revisited.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted patent claims were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional for attorney's fees purposes. The decision continues to narrow the scope of patentable subject matter for data collection and processing technologies in the agricultural sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing data-processing patents benefit from continued robust § 101 eligibility screening, and defendants in weak patent cases may recover attorney's fees more readily.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on agricultural technology, IoT devices, and automated data-processing systems face increased risk that their patents will be found ineligible under § 101.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the infringement and damages findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform constellations used in digital communications while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed the infringement and damages findings. The decision provides important guidance on the § 101 eligibility analysis for patents involving mathematical optimization applied to specific technological implementations in communications standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations of mathematical concepts in communications standards retain enforceability, and damages methodologies tying royalties to standard-essential technology are upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communications standards face continued patent infringement liability, and the partial vacatur creates uncertainty about the eligibility boundaries for standard-essential patents.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a field-standard temperature, and whether the doctrine of equivalents could overcome a finding of no literal infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that the claim term 'pH of 13 or higher' must be measured at the temperature standard in the field (25°C) and that Actelion failed to prove infringement by equivalents. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent litigation involving precise chemical property measurements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from precise claim construction tied to industry-standard measurement conditions, providing clearer design-around opportunities for ANDA filers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face narrower claim scope when claims reference measurable chemical properties, as courts will apply field-standard measurement conditions rather than broader interpretations.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an entity that was not a party to the underlying district court litigation but filed IPR petitions challenging the same patents on the last day of the time bar is subject to procedural scrutiny, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding against FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The decision addresses the procedural integrity of IPR proceedings when petitions are filed by third parties who were not parties to the underlying litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by entities not involved in the underlying litigation, potentially curbing strategic use of IPR by third-party proxies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge competitor patents through IPR face uncertainty about the procedural standards applied when they are not parties to the underlying litigation.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent owner acknowledges coinventorship but is unable to locate the omitted inventor to obtain consent for correction under 35 U.S.C. § 256.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid for incorrect inventorship where a coinventor was omitted and could not be located for correction. The court held that § 256(b) correction requires the patent owner to demonstrate diligent efforts to locate the missing inventor, and Fortress's efforts were insufficient. This decision highlights the critical importance of properly identifying and maintaining contact with all inventors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can leverage inventorship defenses more effectively when patent owners have failed to properly identify and maintain relationships with all contributors to the invention.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers or contractors face significant patent validity risks if they fail to properly document inventorship contributions and maintain contact information for all contributors.
